speaker: Edwin
content:
I'm teaching an undergraduate intro to computer science course next semester and
I need a website for it. Build me the whole thing: a home page, a syllabus page,
a weekly schedule, an assignments page with code examples students can copy, and
a contact section. It needs to work on phones, be easy for me to update weekly,
and be hostable for free. Work through all of it and don't come back until the
whole thing is done and you've checked it holds together.

# CS 101 course website

A static website for an intro CS course. No build step, no dependencies, no server
code — just HTML, CSS, and one JavaScript file. It works on phones, and it is free
to host.

**The short version: to update the site, edit `js/data.js` and nothing else.**

---

## 1. What is in here

```
cs101-site/
├── index.html          Home page (announcements, this week, contact section)
├── syllabus.html       Full syllabus
├── schedule.html       Week-by-week schedule
├── assignments.html    Assignments, starter code, code examples
├── 404.html            Shown when someone follows a broken link
├── css/style.css       All the styling
├── js/data.js          ← ALL YOUR CONTENT LIVES HERE. This is the file you edit.
├── js/app.js           Turns data.js into the pages. Leave this alone.
└── .nojekyll           Tells GitHub Pages not to preprocess anything
```

The four HTML pages are essentially empty shells. Every piece of content —
your name, the schedule, the assignments, the grading table — comes from
`js/data.js`. That is the whole design: **one file to edit, four pages update.**

---

## 2. Editing it

Open `js/data.js` in any text editor (VS Code is ideal — it will highlight
mistakes). The file is heavily commented and organized into eleven numbered
sections:

| Section | What it controls |
|---|---|
| 1. Basic identity | Course code, title, term, tagline, description |
| 2. People and meeting times | You, your TAs, when and where class meets |
| 3. Useful links | LMS, forum, gradebook buttons on the home page |
| 4. Announcements | The news feed on the home page |
| 5. `currentWeek` | Which week gets highlighted — **change this weekly** |
| 6. Grading | Weights table and letter-grade scale |
| 7. Syllabus prose | Every section of the syllabus page |
| 8. Schedule | One block per week |
| 9. Assignments | Title, due date, requirements, starter code, rubric |
| 10. Code examples | The copyable examples at the bottom of the assignments page |
| 11. Footer | "Last updated" date and footer note |

### Your typical weekly update (about two minutes)

1. Change `currentWeek: 1` to the new week number. That highlights the right row
   on the schedule page and updates the "Right now" panel on the home page.
2. Add an announcement to the **top** of the `announcements` list.
3. Change `updated:` in section 11 to today's date.
4. Save, and push (see section 4 below).

### Posting an assignment

Find the assignment in section 9 and change `status: "upcoming"` to
`status: "open"`, then fill in `objectives`, `requirements`, `starter`, `rubric`,
and `submit`. Copy the shape of Assignment 1 or 2 — they are fully filled in as
worked examples. Set `status: "closed"` after the deadline if you want a visible
marker.

### Adding starter code

Starter code lives inside backticks so it can span many lines:

```js
starter: {
  filename: "hello.py",
  code: `print("Hello, world!")
print("Second line")
`
},
```

Two things to watch for inside those backticks:

- A **backtick** character in your code would end the block early. Python does not
  use backticks, so this rarely comes up.
- The two-character sequence `${` is special in JavaScript. Python f-strings use
  `{name}`, not `${name}`, so this also rarely comes up. If you ever do need a
  literal `${`, write it as `\${`.
- To include a **backslash** in Python code (like `"\n"`), type two backslashes:
  `"\\n"`. The existing examples in the file show this.

Everything else — quotes, apostrophes, indentation, blank lines — is fine as-is.

---

## 3. Previewing your changes

**Easiest:** double-click `index.html`. It opens in your browser and works.

The one thing that does not work from a double-clicked file is the **Copy** button
on code blocks — browsers block clipboard access on `file://` URLs. The site
detects this and falls back to selecting the code so students can press Ctrl+C, but
it is worth checking the real site after you publish.

**Better, if you have Python installed** (you do — you teach this course). In a
terminal, from inside the `cs101-site` folder:

```
python3 -m http.server 8000
```

Then open <http://localhost:8000>. Everything, including the Copy button, behaves
exactly as it will live. Press Ctrl+C in the terminal to stop it.

---

## 4. Hosting it free on GitHub Pages

This takes about ten minutes once, then thirty seconds per update.

### First time

1. Make a free account at [github.com](https://github.com) if you do not have one.
2. Create a new **public** repository. Name it something like `cs101`.
   (Public is required for free Pages on a free account. Nothing here is private —
   it is a course website.)
3. On the new repository's page, click **uploading an existing file**, then drag in
   the *contents* of the `cs101-site` folder — `index.html`, the other HTML files,
   and the `css` and `js` folders. Do not drag the `cs101-site` folder itself, or
   your site will live one directory too deep.
4. Click **Commit changes**.
5. Go to **Settings → Pages**. Under "Build and deployment", set Source to
   **Deploy from a branch**, branch **main**, folder **/ (root)**. Save.
6. Wait a minute or two. Your site appears at
   `https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/cs101/`.

### Every week after that

Either edit `js/data.js` directly on github.com (click the file, then the pencil
icon, then **Commit changes**) — no software needed, works from a phone — or edit
locally and use GitHub Desktop to push. The site updates within a minute.

Editing `data.js` in the browser is genuinely the fastest weekly workflow, and it
keeps a full history so you can undo anything.

### Alternatives, also free

- **Netlify Drop** — go to [app.netlify.com/drop](https://app.netlify.com/drop) and
  drag the folder onto the page. Instant, no account needed to start. Re-drag to
  update.
- **Cloudflare Pages** and **Vercel** both work identically to GitHub Pages.
- **Your university's web space.** Most give faculty a `~username` directory.
  Upload the files by SFTP and it will just work — there is nothing to configure.

### Using your own domain

All of the above support custom domains free. If you want
`cs101.yourdomain.edu`, that is a DNS record plus one setting; ask your IT
department for a CNAME.

---

## 5. If something breaks

**A page is blank, or a section is missing.** This is almost always a typo in
`data.js` — usually a missing comma, an extra comma, or an unclosed quote. The site
tries to tell you: a red bar appears at the top of the page with the error.

To see the exact line: press **F12** in your browser, click the **Console** tab, and
reload. You will see something like `Uncaught SyntaxError: ... data.js:214`. Go to
line 214 of `data.js` and look just above it.

If you get stuck, the fastest fix is to undo your last change. On GitHub, click the
file, then **History**, then revert to the previous version.

**The grading weights or a rubric do not add up.** The site checks this and prints
a warning on the page — deliberately visible, so you notice it rather than your
students. Fix the numbers in `data.js` and it disappears.

**A student says the site looks broken on their phone.** Ask what browser and get a
screenshot. The layout is tested down to 320px wide (an iPhone SE) and uses no
features newer than about 2021.

---

## 6. Things you might want to change

- **Colors.** Everything is defined in the `:root` block at the top of
  `css/style.css`. Change `--accent` to your department's color and the whole site
  follows. There is a matching dark-mode block just below it — the site respects
  whatever theme a student's phone is set to.
- **Adding a page.** Copy `schedule.html`, rename it, change `data-page`, add a
  `<li>` to the nav list in all five HTML files, and put your content in `<main>`.
- **Removing the labs.** Delete `lab` and `labRoom` from `meetings` in section 2 and
  set each week's `lab` to `""`. Those rows disappear on their own.
- **Removing the TAs.** Delete the blocks inside `assistants: [ ]` and leave it
  empty.

---

## 7. Accessibility and privacy notes

The site was built to be usable by everyone in your class:

- Works with keyboard only, and with screen readers (landmarks, skip link, proper
  heading order, live region on the Copy button).
- Text scales to 200% without breaking; tables reflow into cards on narrow screens.
- Respects `prefers-reduced-motion` and `prefers-color-scheme`.
- Prints cleanly, so the syllabus makes a decent PDF straight from the browser.

There is **no tracking, no analytics, no cookies, and no third-party requests** of
any kind. Nothing loads from a CDN; nothing phones home. Students visiting the site
are not observed, which is the right default for a course page and avoids a FERPA
conversation entirely.

Done. Here's what's in `<path>`:

```
index.html        Home: hero, announcements, "this week" panel, contact section
syllabus.html     Full syllabus, prints cleanly to PDF
schedule.html     15 weeks + break + finals, current week highlighted
assignments.html  Setup guide, 6 assignments, starter code, 7 reference examples

css/style.css     All styling, light + dark
js/data.js        ← every word of content lives here
js/app.js         Renderer (you never touch this)
README.md         How to update, how to host, how to fix a typo
.nojekyll
```

**The update story.** The HTML pages are empty shells. All content comes from `js/data.js`, organized into 11 commented sections. Your weekly ritual is: bump `currentWeek: 3` to `4`, add an announcement to the top of the list, change the "last updated" date. Two minutes, editable straight in github.com's web editor from a phone. Posting an assignment is flipping `status: "upcoming"` to `"open"` and filling in the fields — assignments 1–3 are fully written as worked examples, 4–6 show the not-yet-posted state.

**Hosting.** Static files, zero dependencies, no build step. README walks through GitHub Pages step by step, with Netlify Drop / Cloudflare / university web space as alternatives.

**Mobile.** Mobile-first CSS. Nav collapses behind a Menu button; tables reflow into stacked cards rather than scrolling; 44px tap targets; code blocks scroll horizontally on their own. On phones the "this week" panel comes *before* the long prose (the aside is first in the DOM and grid-placed back to the right column on desktop).

**Code examples.** Copy buttons use the Clipboard API with an `execCommand` fallback, and if both fail they select the text and tell you to press Ctrl+C — that last path matters because clipboard access is blocked on `file://` URLs, so it fires when you preview by double-clicking `index.html`.

Things I fixed during the consistency pass, since they'd have bitten you: the nav toggle's `hidden` attribute was being overridden by my own `display` rule (button would have shown on desktop); the "when and where we meet" card was placed outside the grid it was styled to span; scroll regions had `role="region"` with no accessible name; assignment/schedule dates cross-checked against each other (all six due dates match their schedule weeks, grading weights sum to 100, every rubric sums to its stated point total — the site prints a visible warning if you ever break those).

Three things to know:

1. **I could not run or render anything** — no shell in this environment. The consistency check was a careful manual read of every selector, data key, and internal anchor, not a browser test. Open `index.html` and click through before you rely on it.
2. **The term is a guess.** You said "next semester" in August, which I read as Spring 2027, with dates laid out from Jan 19. If you meant Fall 2026, change `term` and the 16 `dates` fields.
3. **Placeholders to replace:** your name is filled in from your email, but office location, office hours, both TA blocks, and the LMS/forum/gradebook URLs are all dummy values. The syllabus policies (late days, collaboration, AI use) are written as real, opinionated policies rather than lorem ipsum — read them and make sure you actually agree before students do.

The site requires JavaScript, which is the price of the one-file-to-edit design. Each page has a `noscript` banner explaining that, and the static prose (setup instructions, intro text, nav) still renders without it.

Done.

**One thing didn't match your description:** the site already ran a lab every teaching week — it had **fourteen** numbered labs (Labs 1–14, weeks 2–15), not four. So there was nothing to convert from four-total; the only real gap was 14 vs. 11.

**How I got to eleven.** The last three lab slots were already *"Final project work session"* ×2 and *"Last-minute help, drop-in"* — unstructured project time, not lab exercises. I un-numbered those three. Result: Labs 1–11 in weeks 2–12, plus three ungraded work sessions in weeks 13–15, and a lab still meets every single week.

Changes:

- **Schedule (weeks 13, 14, 15)** — now read "Final project work session (not a graded lab)" and "Last-minute help, drop-in (not a graded lab)". Labs 1–11 are untouched.
- **Grading** — "Weekly labs (best 12 of 14)" → "best 9 of 11", same 20% weight. Weights still total 100.
- **Assignments page** — new **Labs** section between the assignments and the code examples, linked from the page intro. It lists all fourteen lab meetings with week, dates, and title, and opens with an auto-counted sentence: *"Lab meets every week from Week 2 through Week 15. There are 11 graded labs; the remaining sessions are open work time."*

The Labs table is generated from the `lab:` field in the schedule, so the two pages can't drift apart — edit a week once and both update. It counts a lab as graded when its text starts with `Lab <number>`, recounts itself, and removes the whole section if you ever clear the labs out. That rule is documented in README §6, along with the reminder that renumbering means updating the "best 9 of 11" line by hand.

While wiring it I caught that Week 1's `lab` field says "No lab — install Python and VS Code", which would have appeared as a lab row and contradicted the "meets every week" line; it's now filtered out.

Two caveats:

1. **Still no way to run anything here** — this was another manual read-through, not a browser test.
2. **If eleven means something different** — e.g. your term is shorter than the 15 weeks I invented, or weeks 13–15 really do have graded labs and three *other* weeks don't — tell me which weeks lose theirs and it's a two-minute change. My split was inferred from what those sessions were already described as doing, not from anything you told me.
